item.title: Utilizing digital ethnography techniques to expand walkthrough method using participant-generated media
item.dc:creator: Renee Mitson
item.description:
Annals of the ICA · Renee Mitson

Topics: Digital ethnography, Participant-generated media, User-generated content, Digital platforms

Abstract Walkthrough has found modern application as a methodology in user experience scholarship and practice to allow researchers to qualitatively “walk,” step-by-step, through a digital interface and examine functions, communication, implications, and usability. Simultaneously, existing users of digital platforms have begun creating media of themselves walking through properties for the benefit of their digital communities, leading to the rise of user-generated walkthroughs. These user-generated walkthroughs share user experience, provide situated expertise, and circulate knowledge within digital communities. Despite this growth, walkthrough methodology has largely developed within UX and human–computer interaction contexts and lacks deeper integration with social scientific and ethnographic priorities. User-generated walkthroughs in communication research present a unique opportunity to bridge these traditions by bringing the rigor and epistemological commitments of digital ethnography into conversation with walkthrough practice. In doing so, participant-generated walkthroughs center participant knowledge, positioning users as active interpreters who signal what is meaningful in digital environments. This manuscript proposes theoretical and methodological directions for future participant-generated walkthrough research, arguing that digital ethnographic considerations provide the necessary structure for more rigorous and socially grounded applications of the Walkthrough method, while also opening new possibilities for qualitative and computational inquiry in digital spaces.

item.title: Inoculating against fatalistic beliefs: a comparative test of narrative and non-narrative strategies
item.dc:creator: Minyi Chen, Hye Kyung Kim
item.description:
Journal of Communication · Minyi Chen, Hye Kyung Kim

Topics: Health communication, Misinformation, Message effects, Narrative persuasion

Abstract This study compares the effectiveness of narrative and non-narrative inoculation messages in reducing fatalistic beliefs and fostering resistance to conflicting cancer information. A two-phase randomized experiment (N = 572 in Phase 1; n = 332 in Phase 2) tested their effects on counterarguing against attack, cancer fatalism, perceived efficacy, and intentions to adopt cancer risk-reduction behaviors. Compared with control, both inoculation messages reduced cancer fatalism, enhanced perceived efficacy, and increased certain intentions to adopt certain risk-reduction behaviors. Narrative inoculation elicited more counterarguing against attack than the non-narrative counterpart. Inoculation effects also varied by baseline fatalism, functioning therapeutically by immediately reducing initially high fatalism and, more modestly, prophylactically by maintaining initially low fatalism. These findings extend inoculation theory by elucidating the role of message format in sustaining resistance to negative media effects, and by demonstrating the theory’s potential dual prophylactic–therapeutic functionality in a fatalistic belief context.

item.title: The sequential replicant effect in interpersonal sincerity: evidence from AI-mediated apology and gratitude
item.dc:creator: Bolin Cao, Zhenming Li
item.description:
Journal of Computer-Mediated Communication · Bolin Cao, Zhenming Li

Topics: Artificial intelligence, Interpersonal communication, Trust, Computer-mediated communication

Abstract Sincerity, a core interpersonal value that mobilizes emotional resources, faces distinct challenges in AI-mediated interpersonal contexts. Extending the Replicant Effect from informational trust to interpersonal sincerity, this study examines how AIMC awareness and AI involvement cues shape sincerity judgments and subsequent relational responses. Drawing on two pre-registered, two-round studies in apology (N = 546) and gratitude (N = 561) scenarios, we found that AI involvement cues reliably reduced perceived sincerity. Primed AIMC awareness showed a more sequential influence on later no-cue evaluations through AIMC suspicion. High-ambiguity AI cues produced sequential effects only in the gratitude context. These findings suggest that hybrid human-AI authorship may reshape how interpersonal sincerity is inferred and validated, while also showing that the effects of AI cues and AIMC awareness depend on cue clarity and relational context.

item.title: Clarifying the role of authenticity in online self-effects: examining authentic cognition and authentic self-expression
item.dc:creator: Zijian Lew, Jaz Low, Yingzhi Mar
item.description:
Journal of Computer-Mediated Communication · Zijian Lew, Jaz Low, Yingzhi Mar

Topics: Self-presentation, Social media use, Authenticity, Self-effects

Abstract Research on self-effects (i.e., how communicators influence themselves) has shown that people can change their self-perceptions, cognitions, attitudes, and behaviors according to their public online self-presentations. Identity shift theorizing has argued that self-presentations have to be authentic to elicit the greatest self-effects. The present study posited that authentic self-presentations should be conceptualized as two different components—authentic cognition and authentic self-expression—understood from a communicator’s point of view. In a between-subjects experiment, participants were instructed to publicly self-present on their actual social media accounts in one of three ways that correspond to descending levels of authentic cognition and authentic self-expression: with mindfulness (with awareness, balance, and acceptance), with facticity (being purely factual and unemotional), or with self-glorification (with exaggerations and embellishments). Results showed that participants who self-presented mindfully experienced less toxic positivity than those who self-glorified, and less toxic positivity was associated with greater commitment to their self-presentations and greater recalled enjoyment. However, the more narcissistic participants were, the more they enjoyed self-glorification than self-presenting mindfully. Therefore, the study showed that authenticity shaped self-effects associated with public online self-presentation and extended self-effects theorizing to cognitive-affective evaluations of recalled experience.

item.title: History as theory: Jonathan Sterne’s speculative historiography
item.dc:creator: Burce Celik
item.description:
Communication, Culture & Critique · Burce Celik

Topics: Media theory, Communication theory, Media history, Sound reproduction

Abstract This article reflects on Jonathan Sterne’s influence and legacy in media history, focusing particularly on his understanding of history as a mode of theorizing. Drawing on my encounters with Jonathan’s teaching and scholarship during my PhD at McGill, I consider how his historical craft challenged conventional ways of studying media and technology: by reconstructing the objects of historical inquiry, allowing theory to emerge through historical investigation rather than precede it, and attending to the longer historical “currents” through which media forms take shape. Through his work on infrastructures, sound reproduction, formats, and listening, Jonathan showed how historical inquiry could unsettle what appears natural, universal, or inevitable in the present. I argue that this speculative understanding of history as theory remains one of his most important and inspiring legacies for media history.

item.title: How does political efficacy condition clicks on politics? Understanding information-selection behavior in algorithmic feeds over time
item.dc:creator: Jin Wan, Theo Araujo, Natali Helberger, Claes H. de Vreese
item.description:
Journal of Computer-Mediated Communication · Jin Wan, Theo Araujo, Natali Helberger, Claes H. de Vreese

Topics: Political efficacy, Algorithmic curation, Political information, Social media algorithms

Abstract This study uses political efficacy to explain individual differences in selecting political information on algorithmic feeds. Combining survey data and 186 Dutch individuals’ usage histories of Google Discover, a fully algorithmically curated feed, we examined both within-person changes of information-selection behavior over time and between-person differences conditioned by political efficacy in three aspects: the proportion of political information selected by users, exposure diversity as manifested via sources, and proportion of negative political information. While we did not find any longitudinal change conditioned by external efficacy on information-selection patterns, we found that internally efficacious users are more resilient to prevalent concerns about algorithms’ negative influence on political information consumption and exposure diversity. We observed their stable proportions of political information consumption and consumption from increasingly diverse sources over time. Alarmingly, there is a growing divide in exposure diversity between less and more efficacious users over time. Altogether, our study not only highlights users’ agency in navigating algorithmic environments but also underscores the importance of empowering users with account of different vulnerabilities.

item.title: Remembering and re-arranging: Jonathan Sterne (1970–2025)
item.dc:creator: Jeremy Wade Morris
item.description:
Communication, Culture & Critique · Jeremy Wade Morris

Topics: Media history, Sound studies, Academic publishing, Communication science

Abstract The following reflection piece discusses the work and legacy of Jonathan Sterne from the point of view of one his advisees. While it dutifully focuses on Jonathan’s contributions to the field of Sound Studies and on his methods of media history, it also tries, perhaps in vain, to capture a few of the many qualities that made Jonathan such a special, caring and generous mentor, friend and colleague. To distill the abstract even further: We miss you Jonathan.

item.title: Loneliness and the local news environment
item.dc:creator: Danny Hayes, Anusha Trivedi
item.description:
Journal of Communication · Danny Hayes, Anusha Trivedi

Topics: Loneliness, Local news, News consumption, Well-being

Abstract Recent research suggests that changes to the media environment have contributed to loneliness in the United States. This work focuses on smartphones and social media, with the decline of local news receiving little attention. We argue that local news promotes social well-being by informing residents about their communities, fostering attachment and a sense of belonging that can reduce loneliness. We provide evidence in two studies. First, using state-level data and multiple measures of news availability, we show that loneliness is higher in states with fewer options for local news. Second, we find in a nationally representative survey that people who rarely consume local journalism report greater loneliness than regular local news consumers. There is some evidence that the relationship is strongest in rural areas, which have experienced severe declines in local news access. We conclude by proposing a research agenda to further explore how community news may support social well-being.

item.title: Looking good, fitting in: co-trajectories of appearance- and friendship-related identity distress and positive online self-presentation in adolescence
item.dc:creator: Gaëlle Vanhoffelen, Lara Schreurs, Laura Vandenbosch
item.description:
Journal of Communication · Gaëlle Vanhoffelen, Lara Schreurs, Laura Vandenbosch

Topics: Adolescent mental health, Self-presentation, Social media use, Identity development

Abstract Adolescence is a critical period for identity development, often accompanied by identity distress. Simultaneously, adolescents are also preoccupied with presenting themselves as positive as possible on social media, which may reflect and reinforce identity distress. Yet, the dynamic associations between adolescents’ identity distress and positive online self-presentations remain unexplored. Accordingly, this three-wave panel study among adolescents from Belgium, France, and Slovenia (N = 1,697; Mage = 15.14, SDage = 1.78, 57.2% girls) used Latent Class Growth Analysis to identify distinct co-trajectories of identity distress and positive online self-presentation in the domains of friendship and appearance over one year. The findings showed that identity distress and positive self-presentations can follow maladaptive, (high risk) adaptive, or stable co-trajectories over time, depending on the identity domain, adolescents’ demographic, and social media use characteristics. In doing so, the study provides novel evidence on the heterogeneous co-development of adolescents’ identity distress and online self-presentation.

item.title: Rejection of cross-cutting news depends on content, sources, and cultural contexts: evidence from online trace data
item.dc:creator: Claire Wonjeong Jo, Magdalena Wojcieszak
item.description:
Journal of Communication · Claire Wonjeong Jo, Magdalena Wojcieszak

Topics: Selective exposure, Political polarization, Online comments, News framing

Abstract We examine the conditions in which people reject cross-cutting news in naturalistic settings of online comments. Theoretically, we account for article content and source to test whether commenters’ rejection and its intensity depend on whether cross-cutting news (a) is hostile to their in-group or favorable to the out-group and (b) is “unexpected” (from in-group sources) or “expected” (from out-group sources). Methodologically, we use online traces from news aggregators in South Korea (SK; 7,607 comments) and the United States (116,308 comments). We find that most commenters (79% in SK and 64% in the United States) reject cross-cutting news, with left-leaning commenters expressing stronger rejection than right-leaning commenters. Regarding article content, the SK commenters more strongly rejected in-group hostility, while the U.S. commenters rejected out-group favoritism more. Regarding article source, SK commenters more strongly rejected unexpected cross-cutting news from in-group sources than expected cross-cutting news from out-group sources. We discuss the implications of these findings.

item.title: Detour: after impairment theory (for Jonathan Sterne)
item.dc:creator: Lilian Radovac
item.description:
Communication, Culture & Critique · Lilian Radovac

Topics: Disability justice, Communication theory, Media theory, Labor organizing

Abstract This article reflects on Jonathan Sterne’s scholarship and the continuities and detours in his last published book, Diminished Faculties: A Political Phenomenology of Impairment. It also considers some of his longstanding social justice commitments, particularly to labor organizing, and amplifies his call for disability justice in both scholarly and activist work.

item.title: Face-off: facial expression disclosure affects the processing of proxemic norms in virtual reality
item.dc:creator: Kun Xu, Mengsu Shi, Jiayue Li, Zhe Zhou, Yunxiao Chen, Sylvia M. Chan‐Olmsted
item.description:
Journal of Computer-Mediated Communication · Kun Xu, Mengsu Shi, Jiayue Li, Zhe Zhou, Yunxiao Chen, Sylvia M. Chan‐Olmsted

Topics: Virtual reality, Social presence, Self-presentation, Psychophysiological measures

Abstract As virtual reality (VR) technologies support various forms of social interactions, questions have emerged regarding whether and how interpersonal proxemic norms are enacted in VR. Meanwhile, VR’s body tracking features, particularly face and eye tracking, have fostered more natural and vivid communication. However, these tracking features also intensify users’ pressure to manage self-image and privacy. Drawing on lab experiments, psychophysiological measures, and qualitative interpretations, this study seeks to understand how face tracking influences individuals’ cognitive and affective reactions to proxemic norm violation in VR. The findings suggest that although participants perceive proxemic norm violations as improper, physiologically arousing, and unpleasant, emerging norms in VR have subtly shifted these reactions. Participants’ gender and facial expression visibility separately or jointly moderate the effects of norm violation on perceived politeness, identifiability, and social presence. The potential theoretical integration of presence, transformed social interaction, and objective self-awareness is discussed to inform future research.

item.title: Do algorithmic information environments mark the end of media effects research?
item.dc:creator: Isabelle Freiling, Jakob Ohme, Isabel I. Villanueva, Dietram A. Scheufele
item.description:
Annals of the ICA · Isabelle Freiling, Jakob Ohme, Isabel I. Villanueva, Dietram A. Scheufele

Topics: Media effects, Algorithmic curation, Communication theory, Digital trace data

Abstract Algorithmically curated information environments are beginning to challenge both long-standing notions of what media effects look like and our ability to study them directly. Algorithmic curation and microtargeting of content based on users’ behavioral and digital trace data pose conceptual as well as methodological challenges to our understanding of communication effects. These challenges increasingly introduce significant distortions to our field’s current ability to transparently and systematically iterate between theory and empirical testing. In this article, we provide a blueprint for how a systematic, empirical rethinking, and testing of communication effects theory can look like in an era of what we call preference-based information ecologies (PBIEs). Specifically, we discuss 9 current challenges to theorizing that are conceptual and methodological in nature and discuss necessary field developments to address and overcome these challenges. We identify 4 major agenda items that our field must tackle in order to position itself for a future in which all communication processes occur in some variant of PBIEs.

item.title: Towards a Reciprocal Datafication Model: How data flows in our digitally mediated reality
item.dc:creator: Chiara Wüller, Alex van der Zeeuw, Maximilian A. Friehs, Alexander Johannes Aloysius Maria van Deursen
item.description:
Communication Theory · Chiara Wüller, Alex van der Zeeuw, Maximilian A. Friehs, Alexander Johannes Aloysius Maria van Deursen

Topics: Datafication, Digital inequality, Communication theory, Surveillance capitalism

Abstract This contribution explores the deep entanglement of datafication in our digitally mediated reality and introduces the Reciprocal Datafication Model (RDM) as a conceptual framework for understanding how individuals shape and are shaped by data. While data offers opportunities for optimization and participation, it simultaneously reinforces inequalities and power asymmetries, manifesting in phenomena such as surveillance capitalism and data colonialism. Centering the individual, RDM conceptualizes datafication as a reciprocal process across three interrelated flows: the structural flow, which captures socio-technical infrastructures and power relations, the critical flow in which data practices are socially negotiated and oriented towards optimization or surveillance, and the self-relevance flow, where data shapes meaning-making and cognitive processing. RDM bridges individual data practices and broader social structures, while contributing to communication theory by offering an analytically grounded approach to understanding how digitally mediated realities are produced, experienced, and governed, and how individuals navigate emerging inequalities within them.

item.title: Do good chat groups make good neighbors? Continuity and change of norms in neighbor relations under digital co-presence
item.dc:creator: Emilija Gagrčin, Olga Pasitselska
item.description:
Journal of Communication · Emilija Gagrčin, Olga Pasitselska

Topics: Computer-mediated communication, Online communities, Interpersonal communication, Social norms

Abstract Based on interviews with urban residents in Germany and Israel, this study examines how residential instant messaging groups (e.g., WhatsApp, Telegram) reshape the norms of “good neighboring”: reciprocity, distance, and speaking out. Drawing on Blokland’s public familiarity framework and Rosenblum’s theorizing of neighborly norms, we ask how digital co-presence transforms the relational conditions of neighboring and how these norms are negotiated within residential chat groups. We show that messenger groups lower the threshold for mutual support but introduce tensions through persistent mutual awareness, which are thenresolved through norm negotiation. Extending the public familiarity framework, we identify a complementary axis of performativity–discretion that manifests through norm negotiation. Residents calibrate between engagement and restraint, enacting “good enough” neighboring within the double-bounded constraints of a building and a chat group. We contribute to research on digitally mediated neighborhood communication by showing how urban dwellers achieve pragmatic coexistence through calibrated visibility.

item.title: Structural Media Capture: Rethinking media in the Global South
item.dc:creator: Bouziane Zaid
item.description:
Communication Theory · Bouziane Zaid

Topics: Media capture, Media systems, Media theory, Press freedom

Abstract This article develops Structural Media Capture (SMC) as a theoretical framework for rethinking media power in postcolonial settings. Challenging the universalization of liberal-democratic normative models of the press, it advances a de-Westernizing approach that situates media development within historically specific institutional trajectories rather than universal ideals. The article theorizes from Morocco, with comparative reference to the Arab media context, and identifies three overlapping configurations of capture: post-independence state consolidation, market-driven economic dependency, and platform-based infrastructural control. Its central claim is that these configurations interact and accumulate, producing a layered architecture of media constraint. SMC does more than aggregate accounts of political, economic, or platform domination. It reconceptualizes media capture as a path-dependent and multi-level formation through which older regimes of control persist within newer institutional arrangements. In doing so, the article offers a historically grounded grammar for comparative media theory and proposes a framework for analysis across Global South contexts.

item.title: Capturing the media/cultural imperialism debate: Latin American and Anglophone views in perspective
item.dc:creator: Afonso Albuquerque
item.description:
Communication Theory · Afonso Albuquerque

Topics: Media imperialism, Cultural imperialism, Communication theory, Media systems

Abstract The debate on cultural imperialism flourished in the 1960s and the 1970s, closely tied to the process of decolonization, which gained ground in the decades following World War 2. In the 1960s and 1970s, Latin America became a particularly important hub to this debate. This changed, however. By the 1990s, a group of Anglophone scholars—most of them working from the very same countries (US and UK) pointed to as the main agents of cultural imperialism in the world—came to dominate the debate on this topic. This article intends to discuss how the academic Anglosphere captured the debate on media/cultural imperialism, what consequences followed, and what are the prospects for this topic in a new, emerging multipolar world order.

item.title: Post hoc illusion—how the knew-it-all-along effect undermines trust
item.dc:creator: Drew Margolin, Mariken van der Velden
item.description:
Communication Theory · Drew Margolin, Mariken van der Velden

Topics: Trust, Information processing, Cognitive processing, Communication theory

Abstract This article introduces a theory of distrust called the post hoc illusion. The post hoc illusion is a mistaken belief about what others knew in the past. It arises when stakeholders, who have entrusted power to the deciders, infer that the decider “overlooked” facts that were “obvious” and should have been consulted. We show how this effect is a logical consequence of constraints in human abductive processes–the manner in which human minds create and evaluate causal explanations. A research agenda for the post hoc illusion is then proposed, beginning with the identification of key variables that should influence its operation: relevant facts present in the past and theoretical novelty. We then argue that the illusion can be ameliorated through narratives that portray the decider’s state of mind in the past.

item.title: Interlocking technologies of caste and gender: an interview with Dr. Shailaja Paik
item.dc:creator: Sareeta Amrute, Shailaja Paik, Murali Shanmugavelan
item.description:
Communication, Culture & Critique · Sareeta Amrute, Shailaja Paik, Murali Shanmugavelan

Topics: Cross-cultural communication, Communication theory, Gender representation, Interpersonal communication

Abstract This interview with MacArthur Fellow and Taft Distinguished Professor of History and Affiliate Faculty in Women’s, Gender, and Sexuality Studies, and Asian Studies Shailaja Paik builds on her insights in the relationship of gender and caste in India to elucidate communications technologies. Paik describes caste as relational in two dimensions, both between communities and within them. She explains her carefully developed methods of historical investigation to analyze the story of women and caste in India, which include drawing on multiple sources in the vernacular Marathi and English, extensive archival documentation, and oral narratives to make nuanced claims about the complicated relationships between caste, class, gender, family, sexuality, citizenship, culture, and educational opportunity. Paik draws on this research to demonstrate a path forward in investigating caste as a communicative technology and communications as signaling caste in multiple ways.

item.title: Technology-mediated communication among migrant families separated by borders: understanding the tensions of relational maintenance
item.dc:creator: Hyojin Lee, Jennifer A. Kam, Nancy Molina-Rogers, Ricardo Delgado Solis, Amy Gonzales
item.description:
Human Communication Research · Hyojin Lee, Jennifer A. Kam, Nancy Molina-Rogers, Ricardo Delgado Solis, Amy Gonzales

Topics: Interpersonal communication, Computer-mediated communication, Social support, Digital inequality

Abstract This study examined how highly under-resourced Latina/o/x/e families used technologically mediated communication to maintain their relationship when experiencing migration-based family separation. Drawing on relational maintenance literature, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 27 family triads, each including a father, mother, and child (children between 9 and 17 years old). The findings extend past research on relational maintenance by elucidating how structural barriers and culture contribute to tensions in relational maintenance and by providing within-family and between-family triangulated perspectives. Across families, three recurring relational maintenance strategies were consistently tensional: (a) sustaining routine contact, (b) prioritizing real-time interaction, and (c) practicing selective disclosure. The findings from within-family and between-family analyses showed how relational maintenance, which was primarily mediated by technology, became highly tensional under structural barriers and cultural norms and had unevenly distributed costs for family members.

item.title: Exposure to “connective language” in political Facebook posts leads to more enjoyment and less psychological reactance
item.dc:creator: Gina Masullo Chen, Shuting Yao, Lin Zhi, Josephine Lukito, Ashwin Rajadesingan, Natalie Jomini Stroud
item.description:
Journal of Computer-Mediated Communication · Gina Masullo Chen, Shuting Yao, Lin Zhi, Josephine Lukito, Ashwin Rajadesingan, Natalie Jomini Stroud

Topics: Psychological reactance, Political communication, Social media, Persuasion

Abstract In this preregistered study, we experimentally tested (n = 2,032) whether “connective language”—language that expresses openness to others’ perspectives and humility in presenting one’s viewpoints—reduces psychological reactance to disagreeable political messages. Compared with non-connective Facebook posts, a single connective post reduced expressed reactance, counter-arguing, and perceived threat to one’s freedom. Connective posts also elicited fewer negative and positive emotions. Participants found connective posts more enjoyable and they spent more time reading them, although these posts were slightly longer. However, post type did not affect behavioral engagement, such as liking or replying. Our findings suggest that social media platforms should optimize their algorithms to surface connective language, and the public should consider adopting this type of language.

item.title: A comparative test of the protection motivation theory: active and passive privacy protection in Brazil, Germany, the United States, and Vietnam
item.dc:creator: Yannic Meier, Laurent H. Wang, Nicole C. Krämer, Miriam J. Metzger
item.description:
Journal of Computer-Mediated Communication · Yannic Meier, Laurent H. Wang, Nicole C. Krämer, Miriam J. Metzger

Topics: Privacy protection, Protection motivation theory, Surveillance, Cross-cultural communication

Abstract Online companies surveil users around the world for commercial purposes. We advance protection motivation theory (PMT), by categorizing user responses to surveillance as either active or passive (i.e., self-inhibition) privacy protection behavior, integrating privacy literacy overconfidence, and exploring privacy resignation as a moderator. Finally, we adopt a comparative lens by investigating protection behavior in four national contexts: Brazil, Germany, the United States, and Vietnam. Results of an online survey (Ntotal = 2,092) show that perceiving surveillance as privacy threat was not consistently associated with active protection behavior. Rather, self-inhibition was a more likely response to surveillance which may have detrimental consequences for both individuals and societies. Across countries, perceived effectiveness of active protection positively relates to both forms of protection while active protection does not prevent self-inhibition. Interestingly, privacy resignation may not always impede protection. In summary, not all aspects of PMT are generalizable when using a culturally diverse sample.

item.title: What is constant connectivity? The affordances that underlie potential communication
item.dc:creator: Morgan Quinn Ross, Joseph Bayer
item.description:
Annals of the ICA · Morgan Quinn Ross, Joseph Bayer

Topics: Mobile communication, Platform affordances, Communication theory, Digital media

Abstract The idea that people are almost always “connected” is cyclically seen across academic disciplines and societal conversations. In the field of communication, a variety of concepts have been developed to understand this phenomenon of constant connectivity. The current paper integrates prior theorizing through the concept of “connectivity.” Grounded in Schramm’s classic model of communication, we propose a more concrete conceptualization of connectivity through a set of four affordances—mobility, accessibility, availability, and synchronicity—which specify how communication is made possible via channels across space and time. We then outline how both individual channels and overall media ecologies contribute to connectivity. We conclude by considering the implications of studying connectivity along a spectrum from “absent” to “constant,” including how its four constituent affordances can dynamically vary across situations in daily life. Overall, our theoretical review clarifies how (mobile) media support (constant) connectivity and chart an integrated course for studying connectivity into the future.

item.title: Political polarization and press freedom in Africa: a scoping review (of research literature)
item.dc:creator: Samuel Danso, Theodora Dame Adjin-Tettey, Martin Thompson Kwadzo Ntem
item.description:
Annals of the ICA · Samuel Danso, Theodora Dame Adjin-Tettey, Martin Thompson Kwadzo Ntem

Topics: Political polarization, Press freedom, Media systems, Journalistic practice

Abstract Political and media polarization tend to perpetuate divisions and audience perceptions of bias, leading to social unrest and the undermining of consensus-building. This scoping review provides an overview of empirical studies on polarization and press freedom between 2014 and 2024 to ascertain the nature of research, thematic areas covered, and gaps that could inform future research. Aided by Arksey and O’Malley’s methodological framework, 28 articles retrieved from four prominent journalism and media studies databases and publishing outlets that met the inclusion criteria of the study were thematically analyzed. The findings show limited publications of articles in African-based journals compared to their Western counterparts. Ethiopia emerged as a focal point for most of the studies on polarization and press freedom, particularly along ethnic divides. The study identified thematic areas covered to include assessment of the media environment, media polarization and political participation through the media, interrogation of Western conceptualizations and theoretical lenses for understanding media polarization and proposals for African-centered ones, journalists and civil society’s role in holding political actors accountable in polarized environments, and journalists’ professional challenges in polarized media contexts. The study recommends, among others, that future studies further interrogate African-centered conceptualizations around media polarization.

item.title: In defense of qualitative description: reclaiming “little t” theory as a site of knowledge advancement
item.dc:creator: Chelsea Reynolds, Jessica Maddox, Krysten Stein, Nahla Bendefaa
item.description:
Communication Theory · Chelsea Reynolds, Jessica Maddox, Krysten Stein, Nahla Bendefaa

Topics: Communication theory, Research methodology, Communication research, Media theory

Abstract This article problematizes post-positivism’s stronghold on the mass communication canon and defends the use of qualitative description as a legitimate methodology for media scholarship. We present evidence that our field’s gatekeepers have prioritized research that advances what we call Big-T social science theories—those recognizable, named theories with testable, generalizable explanatory power—rather than the context-specific little t theories associated with qualitative description. We link this trend with the systematic underrepresentation of emic research, especially from the Global South. Qualitative description allows scholars to explore emerging research contexts and build trust with research participants, setting ground for future theory advancement. We present a framework for doing qualitative description in mass communication, and we offer clarifications for how this approach differs from other theoretical work driven by qualitative communication research methods.

item.title: Gender in/as communication: a constitutive framework and review
item.dc:creator: Matthew L. Meier, Bengisu Şimşek, Marie‐Louise Mares
item.description:
Annals of the ICA · Matthew L. Meier, Bengisu Şimşek, Marie‐Louise Mares

Topics: Gender differences, Gender representation, Communication theory, Media effects

Abstract Adopting a framework of gender as communicatively constituted, this paper reviews the past decade of research from four flagship communication journals. Across all studies, gender was most often analyzed as an atheoretical class concept, typically a covariate. Where gender was of a priori interest, an inductive thematic analysis revealed seven gender-related topics, with half of studies falling under two topics focused on women’s marginalization. Our deductive coding of communication processes found most papers focused on media, typically as one-directional media effects or content analyses. Few papers considered how gender is negotiated through multi-directional interpersonal and group processes, or across cultural contexts. The paper argues for a shift toward researching gender as a dynamic phenomenon constituted through communication.

item.title: Through their eyes: neural and behavioral evidence for enhanced immersion via point-of-view editing
item.dc:creator: Moran Ovadia, Shiri Davidovitch, Romi Sion, Naama Shoham, Nimrod Keren, Sergei Freedman, Cynthia Cabañas, Dov Rubinstein, Mark Allen Thornton, Jonathan Frome
item.description:
Journal of Communication · Moran Ovadia, Shiri Davidovitch, Romi Sion, Naama Shoham, Nimrod Keren, Sergei Freedman, Cynthia Cabañas, Dov Rubinstein, Mark Allen Thornton, Jonathan Frome

Topics: Point-of-view editing, Narrative persuasion, Media psychology, Eye-tracking

Abstract Point-of-view (POV) editing—the juxtaposition of a character’s gaze with the object of that gaze—is presumed to function as a unique empathic device that dissolves viewer-character boundaries; however, direct empirical evidence remains scarce. This study provides the first systematic functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and behavioral investigation into whether POV editing facilitates shared attention and intentionality. 39 adults viewed 8 original narrative movies containing POV sequences or closely matched control conditions. POV sequences increased fixation durations on characters’ faces and enhanced subsequent recognition of gazed-at content. Neurally, POV editing elicited stronger responses in regions implicated in mentalizing and increased shared, item-specific activation patterns across viewers within areas associated with perspective-taking and goal-directed control. Multivariate decoding further indicates that a character’s gaze induced more robust neural signatures of character identity on subsequent target elements. Together, these findings support a functional role for POV editing in promoting joint attention and shared intentionality in audiovisual messages.

item.title: “Communicating in the Air Force”: the National Society for the Study of Communication, the Journal of Communication , and U.S. military education, 1950–1962
item.dc:creator: Dominique Trudel, David W. Park
item.description:
Journal of Communication · Dominique Trudel, David W. Park

Topics: Communication science, Communication research, Journalism education, Communication theory

Abstract This article explores the intertwined history of the National Society for the Study of Communication (NSSC), its Journal of Communication, and U.S. Air Force educational programs. Founded in 1950 (and renamed the International Communication Association in 1969), NSSC developed a close partnership with the Air Force’s Air University in its early days. The growth of the academic society and the expansion of communication courses in military education programs were then mutually reinforcing: NSSC leaders—including several Air Force officers and civilian consultants—helped define and refine military communication curricula. Air University resources supported NSSC projects, most notably the Journal of Communication. Drawing on extensive archival research and a close reading of the Journal’s content during its first decade, this article argues that these collaborations not only nurtured NSSC’s institutional development, but also shaped a specific conception of communication emphasizing vocational training, efficiency, and the transmission of command.

item.title: Media emotion regulation and executive functions: individual differences in temporal ordering among young children
item.dc:creator: Jane E. Shawcroft, McCall A. Booth, Chris L. Porter, Megan Van Alfen, Megan Gale, Lara A. Maximiano, Elena K Holmes, Sarah Marie Coyne, Hailey G. Holmgren, Blake L. Jones
item.description:
Journal of Communication · Jane E. Shawcroft, McCall A. Booth, Chris L. Porter, Megan Van Alfen, Megan Gale, Lara A. Maximiano, Elena K Holmes, Sarah Marie Coyne, Hailey G. Holmgren, Blake L. Jones

Topics: Emotion regulation, Media use, Executive functions, Longitudinal study

Abstract Using media to help children regulate difficult emotions (also called regulatory media use) is a process linked to the development of children’s executive functions. Although a necessary condition for establishing causality, the temporal ordering of the relationship between regulatory media use and executive functions has not been explicitly studied. In this study, we examined individual differences in the temporal ordering of the association between regulatory media use and executive functions using data from six waves of Project M.E.D.I.A. (spanning 2.5 years old to 7.5 years old). Three classes of temporal ordering were identified: Media Emotion Regulation Driven (7.00%), Bidirectional (87.36%), and Diverging Temporal Ordering (6.00%). Parent depression was negatively associated with the probability of children being classified in the Bidirectional class but was positively associated with the probability of children being classified in the Media Emotion Regulation Driven class.

item.title: Presenting the augmented self: extending sender effects of the hyperpersonal model in artificial intelligence-mediated communication
item.dc:creator: Rui Zhu, David M. Markowitz, Brandon Lee Van Der Heide
item.description:
Annals of the ICA · Rui Zhu, David M. Markowitz, Brandon Lee Van Der Heide

Topics: Artificial intelligence, Computer-mediated communication, Interpersonal communication, Selective self-presentation

Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) has been increasingly used to facilitate interpersonal communication. To provide a theoretical account of how the use of AI may affect interpersonal communication, we extend the hyperpersonal model by conceptualizing AI-mediated communication (AIMC) as computer-mediated communication (CMC) with an AI layer that participates in message production. Focusing on the sender side of the hyperpersonal model, namely selective self-presentation, we propose 2 AIMC affordances (i.e., co-creation and adaptability) and argue that these 2 affordances systematically reshape selective self-presentation by changing the production of both content (i.e., what to say) and language style (i.e., how to say it) of self-presentation. Using traditional CMC as the benchmark, we derive propositions specifying how self-presentation in AIMC differs from CMC, how these differences translate into impression and relational outcomes, and how they affect senders’ psychology. This article results in a theoretical framework called the Computational-Assisted Relational Exchange model, which advances a research program that investigates the changes introduced by AIMC relative to CMC and shows how classical CMC theories can be revisited, reexamined, and extended to account for the mechanisms involved.

item.title: Emotions, social media, and politics: a scoping review
item.dc:creator: Ruta Kaskeleviciute, Andreas Nanz, Irina Dietrich, Jörg Matthes
item.description:
Annals of the ICA · Ruta Kaskeleviciute, Andreas Nanz, Irina Dietrich, Jörg Matthes

Topics: Political communication, Social media, Emotion regulation, Content analysis

Abstract Social media features emotionally laden political discussions among citizens. In recent years, scholars have dedicated attention to the role of emotions in these environments, while being confronted with challenges that come with conceptualizing and operationalizing emotions. We take stock of quantitative citizen-level research by conducting a scoping review of 189 research articles (including 204 empirical studies) in communication and political science published between 2013 and 2024. We find a dominance of experiments and cross-sectional surveys. Studies primarily focus on the United States and Europe. Research often fails to connect to established theories of emotions and faces shortcomings in the conceptualization of emotions. Measurement approaches rely heavily on self-reports and text analysis, each with notable limitations. Based on our findings, we identify key needs for future research: stronger grounding in theories of emotions, clearer definitions of emotions, more rigorous approaches to measuring emotions, greater attention to positive emotions, and inclusion of visual-based platforms.

item.title: Everyone thinks they are cross-disciplinary (and maybe they are right)
item.dc:creator: Jessica Zier, Sijia Liu, Valerie Gruest, Nathan Walter
item.description:
Annals of the ICA · Jessica Zier, Sijia Liu, Valerie Gruest, Nathan Walter

Topics: Communication science, Communication research, Academic publishing, Journalism

Abstract Cross-disciplinary research has become both a promise and a puzzle for the field of communication—a discipline that celebrates boundary-crossing yet continually reflects on its unique contributions and distinct identity. Drawing on a survey of 278 editorial board members from leading communication journals, this study examines how a sample of researchers occupying key mentorship and gatekeeping roles conceptualize and practice cross-disciplinarity across academic lineages: their advisors, themselves, and their advisees. Results reveal widespread support for cross-disciplinary engagement, with most respondents describing their own work as bringing together ideas from different fields. However, further coding indicated that most scholars engage primarily in multidisciplinary rather than interdisciplinary or transdisciplinary forms of scholarship. Respondents viewed themselves and their advisees as more cross-disciplinary than communication scholars in general and their advisors, respectively, while also perceiving junior scholars, doctoral students, and funders as more supportive of cross-disciplinary work than journal editors and senior scholars. Qualitative findings further highlighted themes of disciplinary identity negotiation, institutional tensions, collaborative knowledge production, and the perceived importance of cross-disciplinary research for the field’s relevance and impact. Together, the findings portray a discipline that strongly values cross-disciplinary ideals while continuing to negotiate their meaning and implementation.

item.title: The eye-tracking monoculture in communication research: diversifying constructs, roles, and metrics
item.dc:creator: Jason C. Coronel, David J. Hendry
item.description:
Annals of the ICA · Jason C. Coronel, David J. Hendry

Topics: Eye-tracking, Communication research, Research methodology, Measurement validity

Abstract Eye tracking can advance communication research as the technology is increasingly embedded in everyday devices. However, its growing accessibility also raises a critical question: Do communication researchers use eye tracking in ways that expand or limit the field’s ability to ask new questions, refine its concepts and measures, and explain communication phenomena? We make 3 major points. First, we document an eye-tracking monoculture through content analysis of 61 articles drawn from a review of 34 communication journals over the past 35 years. We find that an overwhelming majority (67%) of articles use eye tracking in the same 3-part configuration of measuring attention alone, using eye-tracking measures to operationalize dependent-variable constructs, and relying on fixation-duration metrics. Second, this monoculture can limit the use of eye tracking in developing new constructs, explanations, and metrics. Third, we propose a diversification framework to move beyond this monoculture. The framework encourages researchers to ask: (a) What else can eye tracking study beyond attention? (b) What other roles can eye-tracking measures play beyond dependent variables? (c) What eye-movement metric could make the relevant process visible beyond fixation duration? The framework is a strategy for opening new lines of scientific inquiry that the monoculture is unlikely to generate.

item.title: Funding, evaluation, and research governance: how domestic structures limit the internationalization of Brazilian communication scholarship
item.dc:creator: Francisco Paulo Jamil Marques, Luiz Otávio Prendin Costa, Andressa Butture Kniess, Manuel Goyanes
item.description:
Annals of the ICA · Francisco Paulo Jamil Marques, Luiz Otávio Prendin Costa, Andressa Butture Kniess, Manuel Goyanes

Topics: Academic publishing, Communication science, Communication research, Research methodology

Abstract Contemporary scholarship on internationalization and de-Westernization of academic research has primarily examined external forces that reproduce inequities between Global North and Global South research outputs. This manuscript offers an alternative perspective by focusing on internal dynamics and context-specific governance arrangements that shape internationalization within a Global South context. We investigate how the international research production of Brazil-based Communication scholars relates to two domestic drivers: (1) public investment from national science and technology funding agencies, and (2) graduate program ratings assigned by the Ministry of Education. Drawing on indicators from SJR, SciVal, and official data, we conducted quantitative analyses of publication patterns from 2013 to 2022 to evaluate scholars’ success in publishing in high‑impact journals. The results reveal a paradox: even as public funding declines, publication in top‑tier journals has increased substantially. We also found a marked misalignment between Ministry of Education program ratings and actual research productivity, as several well‑funded, highly rated programs underperform relative to newer and less‑resourced institutions. Moving beyond explanations that attribute the limited presence of Global South scholars in high‑prestige venues essentially to external constraints (e.g., underrepresentation on editorial boards), this study demonstrates how uneven national commitments to international circulation shape research visibility and impact.

item.title: Thinking, fast, and artificial: processing fluency in AI-mediated relational maintenance planning and its impact on relationship perceptions
item.dc:creator: Bingjie Liu, Jingwei Liu, Lewen Wei
item.description:
Journal of Computer-Mediated Communication · Bingjie Liu, Jingwei Liu, Lewen Wei

Topics: Artificial intelligence, Interpersonal communication, Human-AI interaction, Well-being

Abstract Previous research suggests that the ease (i.e., processing fluency) of generating future relational plans leads to perceptions of greater relational closeness and commitment. Can generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), when used to help users generate relational maintenance plans, increase fluency and thereby enhance users’ perceived closeness and commitment in friendships? Does the anthropomorphism of GenAI matter? Drawing upon prior work on processing fluency and extended cognition, we conducted a 2 (plan quantity: generating three vs. 10 plans) × 3 (agency: internal retrieval vs. anthropomorphic AI vs. nonanthropomorphic AI) online experiment (N = 1,397). After establishing the ease-of-retrieval effects on friendship closeness and commitment during internal retrieval, we found that both nonanthropomorphic and anthropomorphic AI (vs. internal retrieval) increased fluency, through which they further enhanced perceived friendship closeness and commitment. Despite taking a longer time to operate, the anthropomorphic AI induced a greater level of fluency than the nonanthropomorphic AI. We discuss theoretical implications for the ease-of-retrieval effect in interpersonal planning, AI-mediated communication, and human–machine communication.

item.title: Context, script, cue: understanding human–AI intimate relationships
item.dc:creator: Fan Yang, Mengfei Du, Ningxin Li, Qing Yan
item.description:
Journal of Computer-Mediated Communication · Fan Yang, Mengfei Du, Ningxin Li, Qing Yan

Topics: Artificial intelligence, Social presence, Interpersonal communication, Parasocial relationships

Abstract The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into the intimate sphere of human relationships presents a profound challenge to traditional understanding of intimacy, necessitating a critical examination of this technology’s extension into a domain that has always been viewed as deeply human. Through in-depth semi-structured interviews (N = 23), this study examines how human–AI intimate relationships develop in Chinese society at the intersection of traditions and modernization. A three-pronged Context-Script-Cue (CSC) framework emerges, capturing how users navigate emotional investment alongside the artificial nature of AI. By empirically examining how users engage in human–AI intimate relationships, this study offers the new CSC framework for understanding the development of human–AI intimate relationships.

item.title: Desperate for disconnection? A two-study investigation of the Simpson’s paradox in the association between digital disconnection and digital ill-being
item.dc:creator: Mariek Vanden Abeele, Michaela Šaradín Lebedíková, Marijn Martens, Stephen Lee Murphy, David de Segovia Vicente, Kyle Van Gaeveren, David Šmahel
item.description:
Journal of Computer-Mediated Communication · Mariek Vanden Abeele, Michaela Šaradín Lebedíková, Marijn Martens, Stephen Lee Murphy, David de Segovia Vicente, Kyle Van Gaeveren, David Šmahel

Topics: Digital well-being, Smartphone use, Self-control, Digital disconnection

Abstract A conundrum of digital disconnection research is that individuals who report digitally disconnecting more often report poorer digital well-being. This article explores whether underlying differences in trait self-control might explain this conundrum. Study 1 (N = 1,315 adults) shows support for a Simpson’s paradox: Within persons, deliberate digital disconnection from the smartphone is linked to reduced smartphone ill-being, but between persons it links to increased smartphone ill-being. Negative between-person associations between trait self-control and both deliberate disconnection and smartphone ill-being suggest self-control as a confounder. Study 2 (N = 2,000 adults) explores this hypothesis further by contrasting more effortful, deliberated disconnection strategies with disengagement strategies reflecting situational goal-alignment. The findings show cognitive control associates positively with the use effortful disconnection strategies, and negatively with using less effortful disengagement strategies. Combined, the studies suggest digital disconnection takes more effort for some people than for others. This has implications for intervention design.

item.title: Recommending the state: How social media algorithms curate state-created content in China
item.dc:creator: Yingdan Lu, Xinyi Liu, Carl Zhou
item.description:
Journal of Communication · Yingdan Lu, Xinyi Liu, Carl Zhou

Topics: Social media algorithms, Algorithmic curation, Authoritarian information control, Video-sharing platforms

Abstract Authoritarian governments have increasingly expanded their social media presence, producing massive content to shape public opinion and behavior. However, less is known about how social media algorithms curate such content and serve authoritarian political goals. This study theorizes algorithmic promotional curation, whereby recommendation algorithms systematically amplify state-created content, and empirically examines this curation through analyzing 119,064 trending and recommended videos from Bilibili, one of China’s largest video-sharing platforms. Using descriptive analyses, regression models, and Markov chain simulations, we find that state-created content is disproportionately amplified through video recommendations associated with state-created trending videos, and that state-affiliated accounts exhibit strong self-reinforcement. Yet this algorithmic promotional curation is not uniform across content categories, with stronger amplification among state-created news and politics than other content. These findings demonstrate how recommendation systems may subtly serve authoritarian goals, advance a multilateral understanding of algorithmic curation, and extend authoritarian information control frameworks beyond censorship and propaganda.

item.title: Disconnect between theory and practice of decolonizing pedagogies in global journalism and media education
item.dc:creator: Hardi Shahadu, Wunpini Fatimata Mohammed, Emmanuel Erzah Archer
item.description:
Annals of the ICA · Hardi Shahadu, Wunpini Fatimata Mohammed, Emmanuel Erzah Archer

Topics: Journalism education, Media systems, Media representation, Cross-cultural communication

Abstract We explore decolonized pedagogies in journalism and media education, focusing on dismantling the enduring influence of colonialism in media systems and curricula. Historically, colonial powers used media to propagate Eurocentric values, marginalizing Indigenous voices and perspectives. This legacy continues to shape contemporary journalism and media education, reinforcing Western dominance in media practices and narratives. Decolonized pedagogies challenge this by rejecting Eurocentric frameworks and integrating Indigenous knowledge systems, postcolonial theories, and alternative epistemologies into educational curricula. We argue that despite calls to decolonize the field of journalism and media education, more work needs to be done to bring decolonial perspectives to pedagogy in the field, particularly in the Global South. Drawing on curricular analysis and pedagogical experiences from Ghana, we present the pervading discourses on media decolonization and highlight how these discourses can be extrapolated to build a more robust, critical, and decolonial curriculum. Key aspects of this approach include fostering critical consciousness, promoting ethical media practices, and encouraging inclusive, relational learning that respects local and Indigenous storytelling methods. Ultimately, decolonized pedagogies aim to create a more equitable and representative media landscape, empowering students to engage critically with global media systems while centering marginalized voices and perspectives.

item.title: New dualism: rethinking the ontology of media systems through the lens of African liberal democracies
item.dc:creator: Prosper Senyo
item.description:
Communication Theory · Prosper Senyo

Topics: Media systems, Journalism, Comparative media studies, Political communication

Abstract This article draws attention to the emergence of African liberal democracies as a challenge to the existing ontological assumptions within comparative media studies. Using Ghana as an illustrative case, the article argues that the widely understood bifurcation of African media systems can be better construed in the new context of African liberal democracies as a dualism of accommodation of liberal and communitarian normative spheres. This dualism of accommodation becomes a theoretical paradox, when contrasted with ontological assumptions within African media system scholarship that portray liberal and communitarian normative spheres of journalism as incompatible. To resolve this paradox, the article advances “New Dualism” as a new theoretical framework for ontologically incorporating the coexistence of liberal and communitarian journalism institutions in a single media system. The goal is to advance a framework and set a research agenda for conceptualizing the media systems of consolidated democracies in Africa.

item.title: Examining 50 years of methodological diversity within the “Big Four” communication journals from 1974 to 2024
item.dc:creator: Cimmiaron F. Alvarez, Haley Nolan-Cody, Elizabeth Ann Hintz, Kristina M. Scharp, Sandra Vera Zambrano
item.description:
Annals of the ICA · Cimmiaron F. Alvarez, Haley Nolan-Cody, Elizabeth Ann Hintz, Kristina M. Scharp, Sandra Vera Zambrano

Topics: Academic publishing, Research methodology, Communication science, Content analysis

Abstract This content analysis examines how the “Big Four” communication journals (i.e., Communication Research, Human Communication Research, Communication Monographs, and Journal of Communication) have represented qualitative, quantitative, and mixed methods research from their common starting publication year of 1974 through 2024. We analyzed 6,847 articles to examine how the research represented in the “Big Four” has changed over the last 50 years, and what institutions, countries, and authors are publishing the most qualitative and quantitative research in these journals. Our findings underscore the overall dearth of qualitative research published within the “Big Four,” as well as the historical and continued exclusion of qualitative research. We discuss the implications of these findings for the field of communication studies writ large.

item.title: Documentary as slow care infrastructure: afterlives of gun violence
item.dc:creator: Aysehan Jülide Etem
item.description:
Communication, Culture & Critique · Aysehan Jülide Etem

Topics: Documentary, Mental health, Media representation, Social movements

Abstract Gun violence in the US is an endemic condition that structures everyday life, makes loss ordinary, and exposes the insufficiency of existing systems of care. Dominant media representations often detach firearm injury from these structural conditions. This article analyzes recent documentary projects on the afterlives of gun violence. Through critical discourse analysis, I show how documentary can function as slow care infrastructure. I identify four dimensions of this work: critical seeing and listening, trauma-informed protocols, institutional uptake of testimony, and temporal endurance with material effects. Across schools, hospitals, universities, and community organizations, they protect participants, circulate survivor knowledge, support clinical and educational practice, and help build spaces, tools, and relationships for care. Documentary’s value lies in how it reorganizes grief, survival, and accountability across institutions and over time.

item.title: A cultural perspective on online self-disclosure: motivations, adaptations, and co-constitutive dynamics
item.dc:creator: Yujun Lin, Yuqi Lin, Yan Lu, Zhengnan Sun, Yutong Du
item.description:
Communication Theory · Yujun Lin, Yuqi Lin, Yan Lu, Zhengnan Sun, Yutong Du

Topics: Self-disclosure, Cross-cultural communication, Computer-mediated communication, Social media use

Abstract This article advances a cultural perspective that reconceptualizes online self-disclosure as a communicative process. Rather than viewing it as merely individual psychological acts, the framework situates disclosure practices as deeply embedded in broader social and cultural frameworks. Extending Markus and Kitayama’s (1991, 2010) theory, this article presents a mutually constitutive dynamic in which cultural orientations configure disclosure motivations and content, adaptation processes enable situated negotiation of norm variations, and individual practices continuously reproduce and reshape collective norms in digitally mediated spaces. Unlike traditional cross-cultural approaches that treat cultural orientations as static national predictors, the model integrates hybridity, multi-level cultural influences, as well as platform architectures as active cultural systems. This perspective reveals how online self-disclosure both reflects and actively reshapes culturally differentiated selves over time and fosters more inclusive theories of online self-disclosure across diverse mediated contexts.

item.title: Chatting with confidants or corporations? Privacy management with AI companions
item.dc:creator: Hsuen-Chi Chiu, Jeremy Foote
item.description:
Journal of Computer-Mediated Communication · Hsuen-Chi Chiu, Jeremy Foote

Topics: AI companions, Privacy management, Self-disclosure, Human-AI interaction

Abstract AI companion chatbots feel like intimate confidants but exist as part of corporate data systems. Drawing on Communication Privacy Management (CPM) theory and Masur’s dimensional privacy framework, we interviewed users of platforms like Replika and Character.AI (N = 15) to understand their privacy decisions in AI companion interactions. We find that anthropomorphic design lowers disclosure thresholds, encouraging increasingly intimate self-disclosure. As relationships develop, some users engage in simulated co-ownership, treating shared information as relationally held despite recognizing corporate control. Because post-disclosure correction feels futile, privacy management becomes anticipatory and front-loaded—users rely on distancing strategies such as using fake names rather than post-hoc deletion. For some users, privacy turbulence centers less on fears of exposure and more on fears of losing conversational memory—a relational reset feels more threatening than a data breach. These findings extend CPM theory by showing that in human–AI companionship contexts, relational and institutional privacy concerns become inextricably entangled.

item.title: Videoconferencing as a social process: an explication of its multimodal, adaptable, virtual, and interactive dimensions
item.dc:creator: Shruti Malviya, Edson C. Tandoc, Benjamin Junting Li
item.description:
Communication Theory · Shruti Malviya, Edson C. Tandoc, Benjamin Junting Li

Topics: Computer-mediated communication, Digital communication, Interpersonal communication, Digital platforms

Abstract Videoconferencing has evolved into a major shift in collaboration, far beyond its early theoretical discussions in the 20th century. However, the scholarly understanding of videoconferencing remains fragmented across disciplines and anchored in early conceptualizations of audio-video transmission and remote access, and not all its characteristics have equal relevance in the current environment. This creates a gap in defining its current capabilities which span multiple domains, including technology, communication, information studies, medicine, and engineering. This paper explicates videoconferencing as a social process rather than just a technology tool, and identifies its four key dimensions: multimodality, adaptability, virtuality, and interactivity. These dimensions were synthesized from both academic literature, and trends and definitions from key industry players. This study contributes towards the growing conversation on virtual tools and remote communication, and proposes dimensions that warrant contextual emphasis and are resilient to technological upgrades and disruptions of the future.

item.title: Caring with and for the state: the potential of relational transparency research
item.dc:creator: Muira McCammon
item.description:
Communication, Culture & Critique · Muira McCammon

Topics: Political communication, Trust, Research methodology, Public opinion

Abstract In moments of democratic backsliding, the need to build and maintain trust with private contractors and career civil servants, who seek to safeguard democratic institutions and the rule of law, becomes even more methodologically urgent, but the roadmap forward is fraught with risk for both researchers and participants. This article reconfigures the potential of transparency regimes, such as the U.S. Freedom of Information Act (FOIA). Challenging linear and extractive accounts of disclosure and denial, I argue that the FOIA instead constitutes an ongoing communicative encounter, undergirded by hidden labor and power struggles within the U.S. administrative state. The encounter does not always conclude with the release or refusal of documents and data, but adopting a longitudinal praxis of care may allow for a more fulsome understanding of the state and the people working on its behalf.

item.title: Holding the handle: Governance probing as method
item.dc:creator: Muira McCammon
item.description:
Communication, Culture & Critique · Muira McCammon

Topics: Platform governance, Social media platforms, Research methodology, Digital inequality

Abstract Abandoned accounts are becoming increasingly common within the world of corporate social media platforms, yet their afterlives pose a range of challenges for sociotechnical researchers. This article proposes a method for studying the aftermath of institutional disconnection that I call the “governance probe,” which in this instance, involves taking control of an abandoned handle and waiting to see how institutions respond. This technique makes visible the power struggles that unfold between platform firms, state actors, and others across time. In this case, I took hold of @JTFGTMO, the Twitter account previously managed by the U.S. Joint Task Force at Guantánamo Bay, the governing body of the U.S. detention facilities created in the aftermath of September 11, 2001. When the U.S. military attempted to reclaim the handle, I show that Twitter left the handle in the hands of an academic researcher (me). While Twitter reinstated Donald Trump’s account, the probe makes visible how platform power is selectively exercised; some accounts are restored, whileothers are simply abandoned altogether. The method involves three stages: (1) conducting an archival analysis of the account’s institutional history, (2) claiming the handle, and (3) examining whether and how non-use elicits institutional response. As governments migrate between platforms, experimenting with the promise and perils of different corporate infrastructures, governance probing offers evidence of the contestation and uncertainties that institutional disconnection produces.

item.description:
Annals of the ICA · Carlos Alberto Scolari
